source.citation: Philip Meirowitz, "A Case of Acute Poisoning by Arsenic with Subsequent Multiple Neuritis," Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 22 (1895): 178–180. Read at the New York Neurological Society, January 8, 1895.

reported.label: J. W.
reported.occupation: steel engraver; taxidermy as a pastime

complaints: burning pains in the legs and swollen feet, weeks after a poisoning
presentation.course: Took arsenic by mistake from a Bromo-Seltzer bottle he had refilled with arsenic he used for taxidermy. Days of vomiting, thirst, fainting, deafness, delirium. Three weeks later, burning leg pain; two months later, could no longer walk. Seen at the clinic about six months after the poisoning.
presentation.priorTreatment: Iron as an antidote (not retained), morphine injections, poultices; eleven days at New York Hospital.

findings: high-stepping, stamping gait; feet droop, cold and blue
tender feet, legs, and thighs; twitching calf muscles; wasted lower legs
absent ankle, knee, and cremasteric reflexes
loss of touch and temperature sense in the feet, reduced in the lower legs
wasted small hand muscles with reaction of degeneration; absent arm reflexes
periodDiagnosis: multiple neuritis following acute arsenical poisoning

treatments.treatment: static and induced electricity; strychnine sulphate one-twelfth grain three times daily
treatments.response: improving; better use of hands and feet

outcome: Improving under treatment at the time of the report.
quotes: He filled an empty "bromo-selzer" bottle with ar- senic
He walks decidedly better with the shoes on than oft.

modernReading.text: Arsenic-induced peripheral neuropathy, sensory and motor, after a single large ingestion. Slow partial recovery over months to years is usual.

fixed: one large accidental arsenic dose months earlier
acute illness then delayed burning leg pain
foot-drop, wasting, absent reflexes, stocking sensory loss

constrained.rule: accidental: household arsenic kept for rats, taxidermy, flypaper, or a mislabelled bottle

free: who kept the arsenic and why

notes: A chronic version (arsenical wallpaper or Fowler's solution) would need its own card.
